items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "scrotum"?
options: Adds fluid containing nutrients to sperm to form semen.
Holds the testes outside the body at a lower temperature.
Carries sperm from the testis to the urethra.
Carries semen (or urine) out of the body through the penis.
items.answer: Holds the testes outside the body at a lower temperature.
items.markingKey: Scrotum: holds the testes outside the body at a lower temperature.

items.stem: Explain why the testes are held outside the body in the scrotum.
items.answer: Sperm production needs a temperature slightly lower than core body temperature.

items.stem: Explain why many more sperm are produced than eggs.
items.answer: Most sperm die or fail to reach the egg in the female tract, so large numbers increase the chance of fertilisation.

items.stem: Which structure carries sperm from the testis to the urethra?
items.answer: sperm duct
items.markingKey: Sperm duct: carries sperm from the testis to the urethra.

items.stem: State the function of each structure: (i) vagina, (ii) ovary, (iii) scrotum.
items.answer: (i) receives sperm during intercourse; birth canal (ii) produces eggs and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone (iii) holds the testes outside the body at a lower temperature

items.stem: An electron micrograph shows a human sperm cell and part of an egg cell. (a) Explain why the egg has a large cytoplasm. (b) State the number of chromosomes in the nucleus of each gamete and explain why.
items.answer: (a) It contains energy stores (food) for the early embryo before implantation. (b) 23 (haploid), so that the zygote has 46 (diploid) after fertilisation.

items.stem: Where does fertilisation usually take place in humans?
items.answer: In the oviduct
items.markingKey: Sperm meet the egg in the oviduct.

items.stem: Explain how the egg is moved along the oviduct.
items.answer: Cilia lining the oviduct beat, and muscles in the wall contract (peristalsis), moving the egg towards the uterus.

items.stem: Which structure where the fetus develops?
items.answer: uterus
items.markingKey: Uterus: where the fetus develops.

items.stem: A human egg cell has a diameter of 120 μm and a sperm head is 5 μm long. (a) Calculate how many times wider the egg is than the sperm head. (b) A photograph shows the egg 50 mm wide. Calculate the magnification of the photograph.
items.answer: (a) 24 times (b) ×417

What is the name for "the embedding of the embryo into the lining of the uterus"?
items.answer: Implantation
items.markingKey: Implantation: the embedding of the embryo into the lining of the uterus.

items.stem: Explain how the placenta is adapted for exchange.
items.answer: It has many villi giving a large surface area, a thin barrier between maternal and fetal blood and a good blood supply, so diffusion is fast.
items.markingKey: large surface area [1]; thin [1]; blood supply [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why the blood of the mother and fetus do not mix.
items.answer: They are separated by a thin barrier in the placenta; mixing could cause damage from different blood pressures and blood groups, and pathogens could pass.

items.stem: A midwife in Lisbon explains the early stages of pregnancy to a couple, from fertilisation to the development of the placenta. (a) Describe the role of the umbilical cord. (b) Explain why antibodies crossing the placenta are useful.
items.answer: (a) Contains blood vessels carrying fetal blood to and from the placenta. (b) They give the baby passive immunity to diseases for its first months.

items.stem: Explain why some viruses, such as rubella, are dangerous in early pregnancy.
items.answer: They can cross the placenta and damage developing organs of the fetus.

items.stem: Ines writes in a revision note: "The mother's blood flows through the fetus's body." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: The blood systems are separate; substances are exchanged across the placenta.

items.answer: (a) 187.5 g per week (b) 190% (c) Glucose, amino acids, oxygen, ions diffuse from mother's blood across the placenta into fetal blood in the umbilical vein.

items.stem: What is the name for "a hormone made by the ovary (corpus luteum) that maintains the uterus lining"?
items.answer: Progesterone
items.markingKey: Progesterone: a hormone made by the ovary (corpus luteum) that maintains the uterus lining.

items.stem: Explain why the lining of the uterus thickens before ovulation.
items.answer: Oestrogen causes the lining to repair and thicken so that it is ready for an embryo to implant.

items.stem: Explain why progesterone levels stay high if pregnancy occurs.
items.answer: Progesterone maintains the uterus lining so the embryo can stay implanted; later the placenta produces progesterone.

items.stem: In a 28-day menstrual cycle, what happens around day 14?
options: the uterus lining repairs and thickens (oestrogen); a follicle matures (FSH)
menstruation: the uterus lining breaks down and is lost
items.answer: ovulation (LH surge)
items.markingKey: 28-day cycle: ovulation about day 14 (14 days before the next period).

items.answer: (a) 27 June (b) 12 July (c) LH; pituitary gland

items.stem: A graph shows the concentrations of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in the blood during a 28-day menstrual cycle in which no pregnancy occurs. (a) Explain why FSH concentration is high at the start of the cycle. (b) Explain why oestrogen concentration rises between day 5 and day 13.
items.answer: (a) To stimulate a follicle in the ovary to mature an egg and produce oestrogen. (b) The developing follicle secretes oestrogen, which repairs and thickens the uterus lining.

items.stem: A graph shows the concentrations of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in the blood during a 28-day menstrual cycle in which no pregnancy occurs. (a) Describe the changes in progesterone concentration during the cycle and explain their effect. (b) Explain why FSH concentration is high at the start of the cycle.
items.answer: (a) Low in first half; rises after ovulation (from corpus luteum) to a peak around day 21; falls before day 28, causing menstruation. (b) To stimulate a follicle in the ovary to mature an egg and produce oestrogen.

items.stem: Which hormone triggers ovulation?
items.answer: LH

items.stem: Explain how FSH and oestrogen interact in the menstrual cycle.
items.answer: FSH causes a follicle to mature and produce oestrogen; rising oestrogen inhibits FSH production and stimulates LH.

items.stem: Describe the roles of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in the menstrual cycle.
items.answer: FSH (pituitary): follicle matures, stimulates oestrogen. Oestrogen (ovary): thickens lining, inhibits FSH, stimulates LH. LH (pituitary): ovulation ~day 14, corpus luteum forms. Progesterone (corpus luteum): maintains lining; falls → menstruation.

items.stem: Which term is defined as "human immunodeficiency virus, which infects and destroys lymphocytes and can lead to AIDS"?
items.answer: HIV
items.markingKey: HIV: human immunodeficiency virus, which infects and destroys lymphocytes and can lead to AIDS.

items.stem: How does HIV weaken the immune system?
items.answer: It destroys lymphocytes
items.markingKey: Fewer lymphocytes means fewer antibodies against other pathogens.

items.stem: Explain why people with AIDS often die from infections that are not usually serious.
items.answer: HIV destroys lymphocytes, so few antibodies are made; the body cannot fight pathogens such as TB or pneumonia.

items.stem: In a country, new HIV infections fell from 65 026 in 2005 to 23 167 in 2015. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease. (b) Suggest two measures that could have caused this decrease.
items.answer: (a) 64.4% (b) e.g. condom distribution, education, needle exchange schemes, blood screening, antiviral drugs for pregnant women.

items.stem: A health clinic in Auckland runs a programme to reduce the spread of HIV. (a) Explain why HIV testing is important even for people with no symptoms. (b) Explain why there is still no simple vaccine for HIV.
items.answer: (a) People can be infected for years without symptoms and pass on the virus; early treatment slows progression. (b) The virus changes its antigens (mutates) rapidly and attacks the immune cells that vaccines rely on.

items.stem: In a country, new HIV infections fell from 76 373 in 2008 to 47 616 in 2018. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease. (b) Suggest two measures that could have caused this decrease.

items.stem: A health clinic in Dhaka runs a programme to reduce the spread of HIV. (a) Describe how HIV affects the body. (b) Suggest three ways the clinic could reduce transmission.
